# Text as Data: Tokens, Normalization, Zipf {#sec-text-as-data}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** Every number and every code output on this page
was produced by running the code shown, with `scikit-learn` 1.9 and
`tiktoken` 0.13. The tokenizer, Zipf, and vector-space explorers are
interactive.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- turn raw text into model-ready units and defend each preprocessing choice;
- explain byte-pair encoding well enough to predict how a tokenizer splits an unseen word;
- describe Zipf's law and its practical consequence, the vocabulary problem;
- derive a TF-IDF vector by hand and get the same numbers as `scikit-learn`;
- say precisely what bag-of-words can and cannot represent, and defend that in an interview;
- explain why tokenization is where multilingual pain — including Turkish morphology — begins.

## The problem, in one sentence

A model is a function that does arithmetic on numbers. A maintenance log is
a string of characters. Everything in this chapter exists to bridge that
gap, and the bridge has exactly two spans: [decide what the units are]{.hl}
(tokenization), and [decide what number each unit contributes]{.hl}
(weighting).

That is the whole chapter. It is worth saying up front because the
techniques below — bag-of-words, TF-IDF — are sometimes dismissed as
historical. They are not. They are the sparse half of a field whose dense
half you will meet in @sec-embeddings, they still win on small data, they
still power production search, and every interview for an applied NLP role
will probe whether you understand them. More importantly, the *decisions*
they force you to make are the same decisions a modern pipeline forces on
you, only visible.

::: {.column-margin}
A statistician's framing that will serve you for the whole chapter:
preprocessing is not preparation for the model. Preprocessing *is part of*
the model. Every choice below is a modelling assumption, and it belongs in
your methods section.
:::

## From characters to tokens

::: {.column-margin .term-gloss}
**tokenization** — cutting a run of text into the pieces the model will
count. What counts as a piece is a design decision, not a fact about
language.
:::

::: {.column-margin .term-gloss}
**token** — one of those pieces. Often a word, sometimes part of a word,
sometimes a punctuation mark. When a vendor charges you "per token", this
is the thing being counted.
:::

The obvious first move is to split on whitespace. It fails immediately, and
the ways it fails are the entire design space of tokenization.

```python
text = "The pump P-101 didn't fail; it's the seal (again!)."
print(text.split())
```

```text
['The', 'pump', 'P-101', "didn't", 'fail;', "it's", 'the', 'seal', '(again!).']
```

`fail;` and `fail` are now different words. So are `The` and `the`. So are
`it's` and `it is`. Each of these is a decision you have to make, and each
one either merges things that should stay apart or splits things that should
stay together.

### The normalization ladder

::: {.column-margin .term-gloss}
**normalization** — deliberately erasing differences you have decided not
to care about, so that *Pump*, *pump* and *pumps* stop counting as three
separate things.
:::

Here is the standard sequence, in the order people usually apply it, with
the argument *against* each step — because the arguments against are what
interviewers actually ask about.

| Step | [What it buys you]{.pro} | [What it costs you]{.con} | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lowercasing | `Pump` = `pump`, halving many counts | `US` → `us`, `Apple` → `apple`. Loses proper nouns and acronyms. | Yes, unless entities matter |
| Punctuation stripping | `fail;` = `fail` | Destroys `P-101`, decimals, URLs, chemical formulas. | No — strip selectively |
| Stop word removal | drops `the`, `is`, `of`; 43.9% of tokens here | Destroys negation (`not`), and phrases like *to be or not to be*. | Only for sparse count models |
| Stemming | `replaced` → `replac`, collapsing inflections cheaply | Crude suffix chopping. `university` → `univers` = `universe`. | No |
| Lemmatization | `replaced` → `replace`, correctly | Needs a dictionary and part-of-speech tagging, and is slow. | Rarely — subwords are cheaper |

: The normalization ladder {tbl-colwidths="[14,28,40,18]"}

Read the last column with suspicion: it is a default, not a rule. Every one
of these steps is a bet that the distinction it erases does not matter for
*your* task. Lowercasing is free in topic classification and fatal in named
entity recognition. The only way to settle it is to try both and measure.

Stemming and lemmatization both aim at the same thing — collapsing
inflected forms — but they are not the same operation. Stemming
[@porter1980algorithm] applies rewrite rules and does not care whether the
result is a word. Lemmatization returns the dictionary form and needs to
know that `left` is the past tense of `leave` in one sentence and a
direction in another.

The honest modern answer to "which should I use?" is *probably neither*.
Stemming was a workaround for sparse vocabularies, and subword tokenization
(below) solves the same problem better. But you should be able to explain
the distinction, because it is one of the most reliably asked questions in
the field.

::: {.column-margin .term-gloss}
**stop word** — a word so common that some pipelines throw it away
before counting anything. *The*, *of*, *is*. Whether that is a saving or
a mistake depends entirely on the task.
:::

::: {.column-margin .term-gloss}
**vocabulary** — the fixed list of tokens a model is allowed to know.
Anything outside it is invisible to the model, however clearly you wrote
it.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Stop word removal is not free.** On the corpus used later in this chapter,
`scikit-learn`'s English stop word list contains 318 entries. Those 318
words are **0.4% of the vocabulary** but **43.9% of all tokens**. You are
deleting nearly half your text. That is a real compression win for a sparse
model — and a catastrophe if the signal you need is in the word *not*.
:::

### Subwords: the compromise that won

::: {.column-margin .term-gloss}
**byte-pair encoding (BPE)** — a way of learning the token list from the
text itself: start from single characters, and keep gluing together
whichever pair occurs most often.
:::

Word-level tokenization has an unfixable problem: the vocabulary never
closes. Character-level tokenization has the opposite problem: sequences
become very long and each unit means almost nothing. [Byte-pair encoding]{.hl}
(BPE) splits the difference by *learning* its units from data
[@sennrich2016neural].

The algorithm is surprisingly simple. Start with characters. Count every
adjacent pair. Merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol. Repeat.

```python
from collections import Counter

corpus = {"low": 5, "lower": 2, "newest": 6, "widest": 3}
words = {tuple(w) + ("</w>",): n for w, n in corpus.items()}

def pair_counts(words):
    pairs = Counter()
    for symbols, freq in words.items():
        for a, b in zip(symbols, symbols[1:]):
            pairs[(a, b)] += freq
    return pairs

def merge(words, pair):
    a, b = pair
    out = {}
    for symbols, freq in words.items():
        new, i = [], 0
        while i < len(symbols):
            if i < len(symbols) - 1 and symbols[i] == a and symbols[i + 1] == b:
                new.append(a + b)
                i += 2
            else:
                new.append(symbols[i])
                i += 1
        out[tuple(new)] = freq
    return out

merges = []
for step in range(1, 11):
    best, count = pair_counts(words).most_common(1)[0]
    merges.append(best)
    words = merge(words, best)
    print(f"merge {step:>2}: {best[0]!r} + {best[1]!r} -> "
          f"{best[0] + best[1]!r}  (seen {count} times)")
```

```text
merge  1: 'e' + 's' -> 'es'  (seen 9 times)
merge  2: 'es' + 't' -> 'est'  (seen 9 times)
merge  3: 'est' + '</w>' -> 'est</w>'  (seen 9 times)
merge  4: 'l' + 'o' -> 'lo'  (seen 7 times)
merge  5: 'lo' + 'w' -> 'low'  (seen 7 times)
merge  6: 'n' + 'e' -> 'ne'  (seen 6 times)
merge  7: 'ne' + 'w' -> 'new'  (seen 6 times)
merge  8: 'new' + 'est</w>' -> 'newest</w>'  (seen 6 times)
merge  9: 'low' + '</w>' -> 'low</w>'  (seen 5 times)
merge 10: 'w' + 'i' -> 'wi'  (seen 3 times)
```

Look at what happened without anyone supplying a grammar. The algorithm
discovered `est` — the English superlative suffix — as its very first unit,
because superlatives are frequent. It discovered `low` and `new` as stems.
[Nobody told it that English has suffixes.]{.hl} It counted.

The payoff is what happens to a word the model has never seen. To tokenize,
we replay the learned merges in the order they were learned:

```python
def apply_merges(word, merges):
    symbols = tuple(word) + ("</w>",)
    for pair in merges:
        symbols = tuple(merge({symbols: 1}, pair).keys())[0]
    return symbols

for w in ["lowest", "newer", "slow", "widest"]:
    print(f"{w:<8} -> {' '.join(apply_merges(w, merges))}")
```

```text
lowest   -> low est</w>
newer    -> new e r </w>
slow     -> s low</w>
widest   -> wi d est</w>
```

`lowest` never appeared in training, and it is segmented into two units the
model knows well. This is the entire reason subwords won: **there is no
out-of-vocabulary token**. In the worst case a word falls back to
characters, as `slow` partly does. It degrades; it never fails.

has never seen, and `lowest` falls apart into two pieces it knows well. Nothing in
this procedure knows what a suffix *is*.

```{ojs}
bpeMerges = [
  ["e", "s"], ["es", "t"], ["est", "</w>"], ["l", "o"], ["lo", "w"],
  ["n", "e"], ["ne", "w"], ["new", "est</w>"], ["low", "</w>"], ["w", "i"]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bpeTrace = {
  const clean = (bpeWord || "").toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z]/g, "");
  let symbols = clean.length ? [...clean, "</w>"] : [];
  const trace = [{ step: 0, rule: "start (characters)", symbols: [...symbols] }];
  bpeMerges.forEach(([a, b], k) => {
    const out = [];
    let i = 0, used = false;
    while (i < symbols.length) {
      if (i < symbols.length - 1 && symbols[i] === a && symbols[i + 1] === b) {
        out.push(a + b); i += 2; used = true;
      } else { out.push(symbols[i]); i += 1; }
    }
    symbols = out;
    if (used) trace.push({ step: k + 1, rule: `${a} + ${b}`, symbols: [...symbols] });
  });
  return trace;
}
```

### Who pays for Turkish

Now the part that matters if you work in a language other than English. A
tokenizer is trained on a corpus, and that corpus is overwhelmingly English.
The consequence is measurable. Here is Article 1 of the Universal
Declaration of Human Rights, in the official English and Turkish texts, run
through OpenAI's tokenizers:

```python
import tiktoken

en = ("All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. "
      "They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards "
      "one another in a spirit of brotherhood.")
tr = ("Bütün insanlar hür, haysiyet ve haklar bakımından eşit doğarlar. "
      "Akıl ve vicdana sahiptirler ve birbirlerine karşı kardeşlik "
      "zihniyeti ile hareket etmelidirler.")

for name in ["cl100k_base", "o200k_base"]:
    enc = tiktoken.get_encoding(name)
    a, b = len(enc.encode(en)), len(enc.encode(tr))
    print(f"{name}:")
    print(f"  english : {len(en):>4} chars -> {a:>3} tokens  "
          f"({len(en) / a:4.2f} chars/token)")
    print(f"  turkish : {len(tr):>4} chars -> {b:>3} tokens  "
          f"({len(tr) / b:4.2f} chars/token)")
    print(f"  turkish costs {b / a:4.2f}x more tokens")
```

```text
cl100k_base:
  english :  170 chars ->  33 tokens  (5.15 chars/token)
  turkish :  160 chars ->  60 tokens  (2.67 chars/token)
  turkish costs 1.82x more tokens
o200k_base:
  english :  170 chars ->  33 tokens  (5.15 chars/token)
  turkish :  160 chars ->  46 tokens  (3.48 chars/token)
  turkish costs 1.39x more tokens
```

The same sentence, the same meaning, [1.82× the tokens]{.hl} on the
GPT-3.5/4 tokenizer. Since APIs bill per token and context windows are
measured in tokens, a Turkish speaker pays more money for less context.
Newer tokenizers narrow the gap (1.39× with `o200k_base`) but do not close
it. This is a documented and measured unfairness across languages
[@petrov2023language], not a rounding error.

Why does it happen? Turkish is agglutinative: meaning is built by stacking
suffixes onto a stem [@oflazer1994two]. English builds meaning with separate
words, which is exactly what a frequency-based merge algorithm captures
well.

```text
ev             1 tokens  [' ev']
evler          2 tokens  [' ev', 'ler']
evlerimiz      4 tokens  [' ev', 'ler', 'im', 'iz']
evlerimizden   5 tokens  [' ev', 'ler', 'im', 'iz', 'den']
```

Read that output again, because it is remarkable in two opposite ways. The
bad news: one Turkish word costs five tokens, where its English translation
*from our houses* costs about four — and English needed four separate words
to say it. The good news: look at the split. `ev|ler|im|iz|den` is very
nearly the correct morphological analysis — *ev* (house), *-ler* (plural),
*-imiz* (our), *-den* (from). BPE rediscovered Turkish morphology from raw
statistics, without a single rule of Turkish grammar.

One more, to show that diacritics cost extra:

```text
gorusebileceklerimiz            8 tokens  ['gor','use','b','ile','cek','ler','im','iz']
görüşebileceklerimiz           10 tokens  ['g','ör','ü','ş','eb','ile','cek','ler','im','iz']
```

Writing correct Turkish costs 25% more than writing ASCII Turkish. Please
write correct Turkish anyway; just know what it costs, and never benchmark a
multilingual system on token counts alone.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Intuition check: why not just use characters and skip all this?

A character vocabulary is tiny (~100 symbols), never has out-of-vocabulary
problems, and needs no training. So why does everyone use subwords?

**Because sequence length is the binding constraint.** Attention costs grow
with the square of sequence length (@sec-transformers), so a 5× longer
sequence is roughly 25× more expensive. Subwords are a compression scheme:
they buy shorter sequences by spending vocabulary. The tokenizer is the
knob that trades vocabulary size against sequence length, and BPE sets that
knob using the statistics of the data rather than a human's guess.
:::

The three choices, side by side. Every tokenizer you will ever meet sits
somewhere on this line, and the whole design problem is that the two ends
fail in opposite directions.

| | Characters | Subwords (BPE, WordPiece) | Whole words |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vocabulary size | [~100 symbols]{.pro} | 30k–100k | [Unbounded — it never closes]{.con} |
| Out-of-vocabulary words | [Impossible by construction]{.pro} | [Impossible — falls back to shorter pieces]{.pro} | [Constant, and worst for the words you care about]{.con} |
| Sequence length | [5–10× longer, and attention is quadratic]{.con} | [Moderate]{.pro} | [Shortest]{.pro} |
| Meaning per unit | [Almost none — `p` means nothing]{.con} | Partial; often morpheme-like | [A whole unit of meaning]{.pro} |
| Morphologically rich languages | Handles them, expensively | [Handles them well — it recovered Turkish suffixes above]{.pro} | [Fails badly]{.con} |
| Needs training | [No]{.pro} | [Yes, on a corpus]{.con} | [No]{.pro} |

: Three tokenization granularities {tbl-colwidths="[24,20,30,26]"}

Subwords win because they are the only column without a fatal entry. That is
usually how engineering compromises win — not by being best at anything, but
by having no weakness bad enough to rule it out.

## Zipf's law and why the vocabulary never closes

Everything above was mechanics. This section is the statistical fact that
explains *why* the mechanics have to look like that.

Take a real corpus — the 20 Newsgroups collection [@lang1995newsweeder],
11,314 documents, 2.29 million tokens — count every word, and sort by
frequency:

```python
from collections import Counter
import re
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_20newsgroups

docs = fetch_20newsgroups(subset="train",
                          remove=("headers", "footers", "quotes")).data
tokens = re.findall(r"[a-z']+", "\n".join(docs).lower())
counts = Counter(tokens)
print("tokens:", len(tokens), " distinct types:", len(counts))
```

```text
tokens: 2288401  distinct types: 78649
```

Now the shape of that distribution:

```text
top     10 types -> 20.99% of all tokens
top    100 types -> 46.99% of all tokens
top   1000 types -> 71.04% of all tokens
top  10000 types -> 92.50% of all tokens

types appearing exactly once: 38571  (49.0% of the vocabulary,
                                      1.69% of all tokens)
```

Ten words are a fifth of the corpus. Meanwhile [half the vocabulary appears
exactly once]{.hl}. Those single-occurrence words (*hapax legomena*) are
49% of everything you would have to store, and 1.7% of what you would ever
see. This is Zipf's law [@zipf1949human]: frequency is roughly inversely
proportional to rank, which is a straight line on log-log axes.

```{ojs}
  x: {
    type: zipfScale === "log-log" ? "log" : "linear",
    label: "rank of the word (1 = most frequent)",
    grid: true
  },
  y: {
    type: zipfScale === "log-log" ? "log" : "linear",
    label: "times it appears",
    grid: true
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.line(zipfData, { x: "rank", y: "freq", stroke: "#DDE2E7", strokeWidth: 1 }),
    Plot.dot(zipfData, {
      x: "rank", y: "freq", r: 3.2, fill: "#1F4E79",
      title: d => `rank ${d.rank}: ${d.freq.toLocaleString()} occurrences`
    })
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p style="font-size:0.86rem; color:#5B6272; margin-top:0.5rem;">
  Switch to <b>linear</b> axes to see the practical problem: on a linear
  scale the distribution looks like a single spike and a flat line, and the
  flat line is where almost all of your vocabulary lives.
</p>`
```
:::

Three consequences follow directly, and they shaped everything in modern NLP:

1. **A word-level vocabulary can never be complete.** New words arrive
   forever — names, part numbers, typos, compounds. This is the argument for
   subwords, in one sentence.
2. **Most of your vocabulary is statistically useless.** A word seen once
   supports no estimate of anything. This is why `min_df` exists, and why it
   cuts the matrix far more than stop word removal does.
3. **Frequency and informativeness are almost opposites.** The words you see
   most tell you least. That observation is the seed of the next section.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Always look at your top-50 list.** In this corpus the *second* most
frequent token is `'ax`, with 62,043 occurrences — ahead of *to*, *a*, and
*of*. It is not a word. It comes from 13 documents out of 11,314, one of
which contains it 11,147 times: a single junk posting.

Term frequency says `'ax` is the second most important word in the English
language. Document frequency says it appears in 0.1% of documents. That gap
between "appears often" and "appears in many places" is precisely what the
next section is built on — and it is a real bug that has been sitting in a
famous benchmark dataset for thirty years.
:::

## How a word becomes a vector

This is the core of the chapter. We will take four short maintenance logs
all the way from strings to vectors you can compute distances on, and every
intermediate number will be shown.

```python
corpus = [
    "the pump failed",           # d1
    "the pump was replaced",     # d2
    "the valve failed",          # d3
    "the seal leak was repaired", # d4
]
```

The whole chapter in one picture. Steps 1–3 turn text into a count vector and
throw away word order; steps 4–5 reweight and rescale it; step 6 compares. Every
number shown is the one the code actually produces for `d1 = "the pump failed"`.

and `the` is column 6. The two accented boxes are the only places where any
*statistics* happen — everything else is bookkeeping.
:::
::::

### Step 1 — the vocabulary is just an index

There is no meaning in this step. We collect every distinct token, sort it,
and assign each one an integer. That integer is the word's *address*.

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer

cv = CountVectorizer()
X = cv.fit_transform(corpus)
print(cv.get_feature_names_out())
```

```text
['failed' 'leak' 'pump' 'repaired' 'replaced' 'seal' 'the' 'valve' 'was']
```

Nine words, so every vector from here on lives in $\mathbb{R}^9$. In a real
corpus this number is 30,000–500,000, which is the whole difficulty.

### Step 2 — one-hot: a word as a vector, and why it is not enough

The simplest possible encoding of a single word: a vector of zeros with a
single 1 at the word's address.

```text
index of 'pump': 2
one-hot: [0 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 0]
```

This is a legitimate vector, and it is almost useless on its own. Take the
dot product of *any* two distinct one-hot vectors and you get zero — the
single 1 in one vector always lands on a 0 in the other, so every product in
the sum is zero:

```text
pump  : [0 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 0]
valve : [0 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0]
        ------------------- multiply position by position
        [0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0]  -> sum = 0
```

Under this encoding, `pump` is exactly as similar to `valve` as it is to
`repaired`. [Every word is orthogonal to every other word]{.hl} — the
representation contains no notion of similarity at all, only identity. It is
a filing system, not a meaning system: the vector for `pump` says *where the
word is kept*, and nothing about what it is like.

Hold onto that sentence. Fixing it is the entire subject of
@sec-embeddings.

### Step 3 — a document is the sum of its one-hots

Add up the one-hot vectors of every token in a document and you get a count
vector. That is bag-of-words: the multiset of tokens, order discarded.

```text
d1 tokens: ['the', 'pump', 'failed']
d1 vector: [1 0 1 0 0 0 1 0 0]
```

Do it for all four documents and you have the [document-term matrix]{.hl},
the central object of classical NLP. Rows are documents, columns are words:

```text
          d1  d2  d3  d4
failed     1   0   1   0
leak       0   0   0   1
pump       1   1   0   0
repaired   0   0   0   1
replaced   0   1   0   0
seal       0   0   0   1
the        1   1   1   1
valve      0   0   1   0
was        0   1   0   1
```

(Shown transposed so it fits the page — the matrix is 4 documents × 9 terms.)

::: {.column-margin .term-gloss}
**feature** — one measured column of your data. Here, one word. If you
come from statistics, this is simply a predictor variable under a
different name.
:::

A statistician should recognize this immediately: it is a design matrix.
Each document is an observation, each word is a feature, and everything you
know about regression with many correlated, mostly-zero predictors now
applies.

### Step 4 — counts are the wrong numbers

Look at the row for `the`. It appears in all four documents, so it
contributes to every comparison while distinguishing nothing. Meanwhile
`valve` appears once and is the only thing that makes d3 distinctive. Raw
counts give them the same treatment.

We want a weight that is high when a word is frequent *in this document*
and rare *across documents*. Splitting that into two factors gives TF-IDF.

**Term frequency** is how often the word occurs in this document — the count
we already have.

::: {.column-margin .term-gloss}
**document frequency (df)** — in how many documents a word shows up at
all, no matter how often it shows up in each. A word in every document
tells you nothing about any of them.
:::

**Document frequency**, $\mathrm{df}(t)$, is how many documents contain the
word at all. We want the weight to fall as df rises, so we invert it. But
raw inversion is too aggressive, so we take a logarithm
[@sparckjones1972statistical]:

$$
\mathrm{idf}(t) = \ln\!\left(\frac{1 + n}{1 + \mathrm{df}(t)}\right) + 1
$$

Read the formula one symbol at a time. $t$ is a term, $n$ is the number of
documents in the collection, and $\mathrm{df}(t)$ counts how many of them
contain $t$ at least once. The $1+$ terms are smoothing (they prevent
division by zero for an unseen term), and the trailing $+1$ guarantees that a
word appearing everywhere still gets a weight of 1 rather than 0, so it is
down-weighted rather than deleted. This is `scikit-learn`'s exact formula;
other libraries differ in the details, which is a classic source of "why
don't my numbers match".

**Work two of them by hand.** Our corpus has $n = 4$ documents. The word
`pump` appears in d1 and d2, so $\mathrm{df} = 2$:

$$
\mathrm{idf}(\texttt{pump}) = \ln\!\left(\frac{1+4}{1+2}\right) + 1
= \ln(1.667) + 1 = 0.511 + 1 = 1.511
$$

The word `the` appears in all four, so $\mathrm{df} = 4$:

$$
\mathrm{idf}(\texttt{the}) = \ln\!\left(\frac{1+4}{1+4}\right) + 1
= \ln(1) + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1
$$

That second line is the whole design in miniature. A word that is everywhere
tells you nothing about *which* document you are holding, so the ratio inside
the log collapses to 1, the log collapses to 0, and the term is left standing
on the floor weight of 1. It is not deleted — it is told that it gets one
vote while `pump` gets one and a half.

::: {.column-margin}
The librarian's version. Ask for "the book about pumps" and the word *the*
narrows the shelf down not at all, while *pumps* narrows it to a metre of
shelving. IDF is a number for how much a word narrows the search.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Intuition check: why the logarithm?

This is one of the most common interview questions in the whole field, and
the weak answer is "to prevent the weight from getting too big."

The better answer has two parts.

**Diminishing returns.** Informativeness is not linear in rarity. A word in
1 document out of 10,000 versus 10 documents out of 10,000 is a big
difference in specificity; 5,000 versus 5,010 is no difference at all. The
log compresses the top of the range and preserves resolution at the bottom,
which matches how specificity actually behaves.

**It is a probability in disguise.** If $\mathrm{df}(t)/n$ estimates the
probability that a random document contains $t$, then
$\log \frac{n}{\mathrm{df}(t)} = -\log P(t)$ — the *self-information* of
seeing that term, in the information-theoretic sense. Rare events carry more
information, and the log is not a trick for making numbers smaller; it is what
information *is*. Robertson's paper [@robertson2004understanding] is the
careful treatment, and the honest history is that Spärck Jones proposed IDF
on empirical grounds in 1972 and the theory was reverse-engineered later.

**And Zipf closes the loop.** Word frequencies are roughly log-linear in
rank, so a log of frequency is roughly linear in rank. The log is the
transformation that makes a Zipfian variable behave like an ordinary one —
exactly the reason you log-transform income or city size.
:::

Here are the document frequencies and IDF values for our corpus, computed by
hand and then checked against the library:

```python
import numpy as np

n = len(corpus)
df = (X.toarray() > 0).sum(axis=0)
idf_manual = np.log((1 + n) / (1 + df)) + 1
```

```text
          df     idf
failed     2  1.5108
leak       1  1.9163
pump       2  1.5108
repaired   1  1.9163
replaced   1  1.9163
seal       1  1.9163
the        4  1.0000
valve      1  1.9163
was        2  1.5108

sklearn idf_: [1.5108 1.9163 1.5108 1.9163 1.9163 1.9163 1. 1.9163 1.5108]
max abs diff vs manual: 0.0
```

`the` is in all four documents and lands exactly on the floor of 1.0. Every
word unique to one document gets 1.9163. The ordering is the point: the
weight is a monotone decreasing function of how many documents a word
appears in.

On the real corpus the spread is much larger:

```text
the            df=  9477  df/N= 0.838  idf= 1.18
is             df=  7034  df/N= 0.622  idf= 1.48
car            df=   394  df/N= 0.035  idf= 4.35
encryption     df=   169  df/N= 0.015  idf= 5.20
gravitational  df=     8  df/N= 0.001  idf= 8.14
```


```{ojs}
//| echo: false
idfCurve = {
  const N = 11314, pts = [];
  for (let i = 1; i <= 400; i++) {
    const share = i / 400;
    const df = Math.max(1, Math.round(share * N));
    pts.push({ share, idf: Math.log((1 + N) / (1 + df)) + 1 });
  }
  return pts;
}
```

```{ojs}
  const N = 11314, df = Math.max(1, Math.round(dfShare * N));
  return { share: dfShare, df, idf: Math.log((1 + N) / (1 + df)) + 1 };
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p style="font-size:0.86rem; color:#5B6272; margin-top:0.4rem;">
  The dashed line is the floor at idf = 1: a word in every document is
  down-weighted, never deleted. Notice how flat the curve is above ~20% —
  once a word is common, getting commoner barely changes anything. All the
  action is in the first few percent, which is where content words live.
</p>`
```
:::

### Step 5 — multiply, then normalize

::: {.column-margin .term-gloss}
**TF-IDF** — score each word in a document by how often it appears here,
divided down by how widely it appears everywhere. Frequent-and-rare wins;
frequent-and-everywhere loses.
:::

TF-IDF is the product, computed cell by cell. For d1 (`the pump failed`):

```text
counts        : [1 0 1 0 0 0 1 0 0]
times idf     : [1.5108 0. 1.5108 0. 0. 0. 1. 0. 0.]
l2 norm       : 2.3591
normalized    : [0.6404 0. 0.6404 0. 0. 0. 0.4239 0. 0.]
sklearn row d1: [0.6404 0. 0.6404 0. 0. 0. 0.4239 0. 0.]
```

That last pair of lines is the point of this whole section: the hand
computation and `TfidfVectorizer` agree to every digit. There is no magic in
the library.

Follow one row all the way through. d1 is `the pump failed`, so three
positions are non-zero, each with a count of 1. Multiply each by its IDF and
you get $1.5108$ for `failed`, $1.5108$ for `pump`, and $1.0000$ for `the`.
The length of that vector is the ordinary Pythagorean one, extended to nine
dimensions — square, add, take the root:

$$
\lVert v \rVert_2 = \sqrt{1.5108^2 + 1.5108^2 + 1.0000^2}
= \sqrt{2.2825 + 2.2825 + 1.0000} = \sqrt{5.5650} = 2.3590
$$

The six zero entries contribute nothing, which is why this stays cheap even
when the vocabulary has 200,000 columns. Divide through:

$$
\frac{1.5108}{2.3590} = 0.6404
\qquad
\frac{1.0000}{2.3590} = 0.4239
$$

and those are exactly the numbers `TfidfVectorizer` printed above.

That final division by $\lVert v \rVert_2$ is [L2 normalization]{.hl}, and it
is not cosmetic. Without it, a long document has a large vector simply for
being long, and every similarity comparison becomes a comparison of document
lengths. Normalizing puts every document on the unit sphere, so only
*direction* — the mix of words — carries information.

The particular combination you have just built — term frequency, times
inverse document frequency, then length-normalized — is not the only one
anyone tried. Salton and Buckley [@salton1988term] compared a large family of
weighting schemes empirically and this is roughly the one that won, which is
why it became the default in every library you will touch.

::: {.column-margin}
Think of it as converting counts into *proportions of attention*. A 50-word
report and a 5,000-word report both end up spending a total of one unit of
attention; the question becomes how they divide it, not how much they have.
:::

### Step 6 — comparing documents with cosine similarity

::: {.column-margin .term-gloss}
**cosine similarity** — how closely two documents point in the same
direction, ignoring how long they are. It is why a two-line note and a
ten-page report can still count as being about the same thing.
:::

Two normalized vectors are compared by their dot product, which is the
cosine of the angle between them: 1 means identical direction, 0 means no
shared vocabulary.

$$
\cos(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a \rVert \, \lVert b \rVert}
= \sum_{i} a_i b_i \quad \text{(when both are already unit length)}
$$

**Compute one cell by hand.** d1 is `the pump failed` and d3 is
`the valve failed`; they share `failed` and `the` and disagree everywhere
else. Only positions where *both* vectors are non-zero can contribute, so the
whole nine-dimensional sum has exactly two live terms:

$$
\cos(\text{d1}, \text{d3}) =
\underbrace{0.6404 \times 0.5729}_{\texttt{failed}} +
\underbrace{0.4239 \times 0.3792}_{\texttt{the}}
= 0.3669 + 0.1607 = 0.528
$$

Notice how uneven that is. `failed` supplies 70% of the similarity and
`the` supplies 30%, even though each word occurs exactly once in each
document. Under raw counts they would have contributed equally. [The
weighting is what decides which shared word counts as evidence.]{.hl}

```python
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
print(cosine_similarity(T).round(3))
```

```text
       d1     d2     d3     d4          <- TF-IDF
d1  1.000  0.458  0.528  0.112
d2  0.458  1.000  0.125  0.286
d3  0.528  0.125  1.000  0.100
d4  0.112  0.286  0.100  1.000

       d1     d2     d3     d4          <- raw counts
d1  1.000  0.577  0.667  0.258
d2  0.577  1.000  0.289  0.447
d3  0.667  0.289  1.000  0.258
d4  0.258  0.447  0.258  1.000
```

Compare the two panels. Under raw counts, d1 and d4 look 26% similar — but
they share only the word `the`. TF-IDF correctly collapses that to 11%.
Every pair drops, and the pairs that drop most are the ones whose only
common ground was a stop word.

::::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Intuition check: why cosine and not Euclidean distance?

Because Euclidean distance is dominated by document length. A 50-word
incident report and a 5,000-word one about the identical failure differ
enormously in vector *magnitude* and hardly at all in *direction*. Cosine
looks only at direction, so it asks "what is this document about?" rather
than "how much of it is there?"

The simplest way to hold this: after L2 normalization, all vectors lie on
the unit sphere, and there cosine similarity and Euclidean distance are
monotonically related —
$\lVert a - b \rVert^2 = 2 - 2\cos(a,b)$. So on normalized vectors the
choice does not matter. On unnormalized vectors it matters enormously.
That equivalence is the answer interviewers are usually fishing for.

Check it against the figure. The angle between $a$ and $c$ gives
$\cos = 0.651$, so $\lVert a - c \rVert^2 = 2 - 2(0.651) = 0.698$ and the
distance is $\sqrt{0.698} = 0.836$. Before normalization that same pair was
3.16 apart; after normalization it is 0.836, and — this is the part that
matters — the *ordering* of every pair now agrees with cosine.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Where $2 - 2\cos$ comes from

Two lines of algebra, and they are worth doing once because the identity
turns up again in @sec-embeddings whenever someone swaps a cosine index for
an L2 index and expects the same neighbours.

Expand the squared distance the way you would expand $(x-y)^2$, except that
the products are dot products:

$$
\lVert a - b \rVert^2 = (a - b) \cdot (a - b)
= a \cdot a - 2\,(a \cdot b) + b \cdot b
$$

Now use what normalization bought us. A vector dotted with itself is its
squared length, and every normalized vector has length exactly 1, so
$a \cdot a = 1$ and $b \cdot b = 1$. And since both are unit length, their
dot product *is* the cosine. Substitute:

$$
\lVert a - b \rVert^2 = 1 - 2\cos(a,b) + 1 = 2 - 2\cos(a,b)
$$

Distance is a strictly decreasing function of similarity: as the cosine
climbs from 0 to 1, the squared distance falls from 2 to 0. So a
nearest-neighbour search under Euclidean distance and one under cosine
return the same ranked list — **provided the vectors were normalized
first**. Skip the normalization and the two disagree, and a retrieval index
built on L2 distance will quietly start ranking by document length instead
of by topic.
:::

## What bag-of-words cannot do

Now the limits — and they are severe enough that the rest of the book
exists to fix them.

**It cannot represent word order.** Not "represents it poorly" — cannot
represent it at all:

```python
pair = ["the pump failed and the valve is fine",
        "the valve failed and the pump is fine"]
```

```text
vocabulary: ['and','failed','fine','is','pump','the','valve']
row 1: [1 1 1 1 1 2 1]
row 2: [1 1 1 1 1 2 1]
vectors identical: True
cosine similarity: 1.0
```

Two reports naming opposite pieces of failed equipment are the *same point
in space*. No classifier, however good, can separate them, because the
information was destroyed before the classifier saw it.

n-grams buy back a little. Using pairs of adjacent words instead of single
words:

```text
bigram vocabulary: ['and the','failed and','is fine','pump failed',
                    'pump is','the pump','the valve','valve failed','valve is']
cosine similarity: 0.714
vocabulary size: unigrams 7 -> bigrams 9
```

Now they are distinguishable. But notice the cost: the vocabulary grew, and
on a real corpus it explodes — in the experiment below, adding bigrams took
the feature count from 32,318 to 249,522, a 7.7× increase, *and made
accuracy worse*. n-grams are a local patch, not a solution. The real fix is
@sec-transformers.

**It cannot handle negation.** This one costs real money in production:

```text
"no leak was found"  vs  "a leak was found"
cosine similarity: 0.866
```

Two sentences with opposite operational meaning are 87% similar. If your
stop word list contains *no* — and most default lists do — they become 100%
similar. This is the single most common way a text classifier silently fails
a safety-critical review.

**It cannot handle synonymy or polysemy.** `pump failed` and `pump broke`
share nothing beyond `pump`. `Apple` the company and `apple` the fruit are
the same column. Every word is its own island, exactly as we saw with
one-hot vectors in Step 2 — and that is the problem @sec-embeddings solves.

## Does any of this still matter?

Yes, and you should be able to say why with numbers rather than opinion.
Here is a real experiment: four newsgroups, 2,327 training documents, 1,550
test documents, logistic regression, nothing tuned.

```python
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_20newsgroups
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer, TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

cats = ["sci.med", "sci.space", "rec.autos", "talk.politics.guns"]
drop = ("headers", "footers", "quotes")
train = fetch_20newsgroups(subset="train", categories=cats, remove=drop)
test = fetch_20newsgroups(subset="test", categories=cats, remove=drop)

setups = {
    "raw counts": CountVectorizer(),
    "counts + stop words": CountVectorizer(stop_words="english"),
    "tf-idf": TfidfVectorizer(),
    "tf-idf + stop words": TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english"),
    "tf-idf + bigrams": TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2)),
    "tf-idf + sublinear tf": TfidfVectorizer(sublinear_tf=True),
}

for name, vec in setups.items():
    clf = make_pipeline(vec, LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=0))
    clf.fit(train.data, train.target)
    acc = accuracy_score(test.target, clf.predict(test.data))
    print(f"{name:<24} accuracy {acc:.3f}   "
          f"features {len(clf[0].get_feature_names_out()):>7}")
```

```text
raw counts               accuracy 0.767   features   32318
counts + stop words      accuracy 0.795   features   32014
tf-idf                   accuracy 0.831   features   32318
tf-idf + stop words      accuracy 0.853   features   32014
tf-idf + bigrams         accuracy 0.819   features  249522
tf-idf + sublinear tf    accuracy 0.843   features   32318
```

Read those six lines carefully, because they contain four lessons:

1. **TF-IDF is worth 6.4 accuracy points over raw counts**, for free, with no
   extra data and no tuning. The weighting is not decoration.
2. **Stop word removal helps here** (+2.2 points) — on topic classification,
   where function words genuinely carry no signal. It would hurt on
   sentiment or negation detection. There is no universal answer.
3. **Bigrams made it worse** while multiplying the feature count by 7.7.
   More features is not more information; it is more variance.
4. **`sublinear_tf` helps** (0.843 vs 0.831). That option replaces the raw
   count with $1 + \log(\text{tf})$ — the same diminishing-returns argument
   we made for IDF, applied to the term-frequency side.

The other reason to care is that the model is *readable*. Ask a
TF-IDF-plus-logistic-regression model what it learned and it will tell you,
in words:

```text
rec.autos            car, cars, engine, ford, oil, dealer, drive, price
sci.med              msg, doctor, disease, medical, pain, patients, treatment
sci.space            space, nasa, orbit, moon, launch, earth, spacecraft
talk.politics.guns   gun, guns, weapons, fbi, law, government, firearms
```

No transformer will hand you that table. When you have to defend a model to
a safety board, a regulator, or a sceptical plant manager, this matters more
than four points of accuracy.

And the engineering is hard to beat:

```text
shape: (2327, 32318)
stored non-zeros: 234281
density: 0.312%
dense float64 would need :    601.6 MB
sparse csr actually needs:      2.8 MB
ratio: 213x
```

The matrix is 99.7% zeros, so a sparse representation stores it in 2.8 MB
instead of 601.6 MB. Training takes seconds on a laptop, inference is a
sparse dot product, and there is no GPU anywhere in the story.

Putting the whole chapter's evidence in one place:

| [Why bag-of-words survives]{.pro} | [Why it is not enough]{.con} |
|---|---|
| **Fast and tiny.** 2.8 MB for 2,327 documents; seconds to train; no GPU. | **No word order.** *pump failed, valve fine* and *valve failed, pump fine* are the same vector. |
| **Legible.** The model names its own features — `gun`, `orbit`, `doctor`. Defensible to a regulator. | **No synonymy.** `car` and `automobile` are as unrelated as `car` and `banana`. Exact match or nothing. |
| **Strong baseline.** 0.853 here, and it beat averaged embeddings in @sec-embeddings — then beat them again on Turkish data in @sec-bake-off. | **No polysemy.** One column for `bank`, whatever it meant. |
| **No training data beyond your own.** Nothing pretrained, nothing downloaded, no vendor. | **Vocabulary never closes.** New documents bring new words your matrix has no column for. |
| **Deterministic and debuggable.** The same input gives the same output, and you can trace why. | **Negation is invisible.** Removing stop words deletes `not`; keeping them does not help much either. |

: Bag-of-words, honestly {tbl-colwidths="[50,50]"}

The right reading is not "old technology, still surprisingly good." It is
that the left column and the right column describe *different tasks*. When
the words that matter are literally present in the text and you need speed
and an audit trail, this is not a fallback — it is the correct answer. When
meaning depends on order, context, or a word you did not anticipate, no
amount of tuning on the left column will save you, and you need
@sec-embeddings and everything after it.

### Where this is actually deployed

None of the following are old history, and each one is documented
by the company that built it:

- **Ticket triage at Uber.** COTA, Uber's customer support system, runs the
  pipeline from this chapter almost line for line: clean, tokenize, remove
  stop words, lemmatize, TF-IDF, reduce with LSA, then rank candidate
  solutions by cosine similarity to the ticket [@uber2018cota]. It cut ticket
  resolution time by around 10%, and the write-up notes that the
  cosine-similarity ranker beat using the topic vectors directly by 25%
  relative accuracy — because the raw vectors were too sparse. That is this
  chapter's sparsity problem, in production, with a number attached.
- **Search ranking.** Lucene, and therefore Elasticsearch and OpenSearch,
  scores documents with BM25 — a direct descendant of TF-IDF that adds
  document-length normalization and saturating term frequency
  [@robertson2009probabilistic]. Elastic's
  [Practical BM25](https://www.elastic.co/blog/practical-bm25-part-2-the-bm25-algorithm-and-its-variables)
  series explains the formula and its two tuning constants better than most
  textbooks. If you have ever used a site search box, you have used this.
- **Google's own text classification guide** still recommends this
  representation [@google2022textclassification]: it reports TF-IDF n-grams
  as the most accurate of the encodings it compares, and observes that
  accuracy peaks around 20,000 features, beyond which extra features
  contribute nothing and eventually cause overfitting. Our bigram result —
  249,522 features, *worse* accuracy — is the same finding on a smaller
  corpus.
- **Hybrid retrieval for RAG.** Modern retrieval stacks combine dense
  embedding search with sparse BM25 search, because the sparse half catches
  the exact matches — part numbers, error codes, surnames — that embeddings
  blur together. You will build one in @sec-rag.
- **Spam and abuse filtering at scale.** Sparse text features remain a
  first-line filter because they are cheap enough to run on every message and
  retrain in minutes when attackers change tactics. The feature-hashing trick
  [@weinberger2009feature] is what makes this work without ever materializing
  a vocabulary.
- **Near-duplicate detection.** Google's web-crawl deduplication
  [@manku2007detecting] runs on shingles and hashing, not neural networks,
  because it has to work over billions of documents. Shingles are word or
  character n-grams — the front half of this chapter.

The practical rule: reach for TF-IDF when your labels are few, your
documents are long, your vocabulary is technical and exact-match matters, or
when you need a baseline by this afternoon. [Always build the TF-IDF
baseline first.]{.hl} If your transformer cannot beat it, you have learned
something important about your data, and you have learned it cheaply.

## Intuition checks

Answer these before reading the answer. If you can answer all six, you
understand this chapter better than the code implies.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your TF-IDF matrix has 200,000 columns and 5,000 rows. Should you worry?

Not for the reason you think. The matrix is sparse, so memory is fine —
storage scales with the number of *non-zeros*, not with rows × columns.

The real worry is statistical: 200,000 parameters estimated from 5,000
observations. That is a `p ≫ n` problem, and it is the situation every
statistician has been trained to fear. The answers are the usual ones —
strong regularization (L2 or L1), and cutting the feature count with
`min_df`. The Zipf section explains why that second lever is so effective:
most of the vocabulary occurs too rarely to support any estimate. On the
four-category corpus from the classification experiment above, `min_df=5`
takes the vocabulary from 32,318 down to 6,281 — 81% of the columns gone.

Do not mistake that for a free lunch. Those deleted columns still carry
11.6% of the token occurrences, so this is not purely hapax pruning, and
whether the trade is worth it is an empirical question rather than a rule.
Exercise 4 asks you to measure it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Should IDF be computed on the training set or on all your data?

On the training set only, then applied unchanged to test data. IDF is a
parameter estimated from data, so computing it over train + test leaks
information about the test distribution into your features.

In `scikit-learn` this is exactly what `fit_transform` on train and
`transform` on test does — and it is why calling `fit_transform` twice is a
real and common bug. In production the same logic says the IDF vector is a
model artifact you version and ship, not something you recompute per batch;
otherwise your features drift silently as traffic changes.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. A word appears in every document. What is its TF-IDF weight?

With `scikit-learn`'s smoothed formula, $\mathrm{df} = n$ gives
$\ln\frac{1+n}{1+n} + 1 = 1$, so it survives with weight 1 and is then
shrunk relative to rarer terms by L2 normalization.

With the textbook unsmoothed formula $\log(n/\mathrm{df})$ it would be
exactly 0 — the term is deleted. Knowing that the two conventions differ,
and that `smooth_idf=True` is the default, is the kind of detail that
separates someone who has used the tool from someone who has read about it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Why do we normalize document vectors but not feature columns?

Because the two normalizations answer different questions. L2 row
normalization removes document *length* so that comparisons are about topic
rather than size.

Column standardization — subtracting the mean of each word — would be a
disaster here: it destroys sparsity. Subtracting a non-zero mean from a
column that is 99.7% zeros makes every one of those zeros non-zero, and your
2.8 MB matrix becomes 601.6 MB. Sparsity is not an implementation detail; it
is a constraint that dictates which operations you are allowed to perform.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Your search engine returns nothing for the part number "P-101". Why?

Almost certainly your tokenizer. `scikit-learn`'s default
`token_pattern=r"(?u)\b\w\w+\b"` requires two or more word characters and
does not cross the hyphen:

```text
default    : ['101', '102', 'pump', 'tripped']
custom     : ['p-101', 'p-102', 'pump', 'tripped']
```

Your equipment tag `P-101` silently became `101`, and `P-102` also became a
bare number — so the two are now nearly indistinguishable. In technical
domains this class of bug is more damaging than any choice of model. It is
also invisible: nothing errors, accuracy just quietly sits lower than it
should.

The habit that prevents it: after fitting any vectorizer, print
`get_feature_names_out()` and read it. Actually read it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. When is a bag-of-words model the *right* choice in 2026?

When at least two of these hold: you have very few labelled examples per
class; your vocabulary is domain-specific and exact matching matters (part
numbers, gene names, legal citations); you must explain every prediction to
someone with authority over you; you have no GPU or a hard latency budget;
or your documents are long and topical rather than short and nuanced.

And unconditionally: as the baseline. A team that reports "our transformer
gets 0.91" without reporting that TF-IDF gets 0.89 has not measured
anything (@sec-llm-eval).
:::

## Interview questions

Text representation is the most reliably examined topic in applied NLP
interviews, because it is where a candidate either has mental models or has
memorized library calls. Below, the questions are grouped by what they are
really testing.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On attribution — please read this once.** You will find a great many pages
online headed "NLP questions asked at Google and Amazon". Essentially all of
them are search-engine content with no evidence behind the claim. Companies
do not publish their question banks, candidates sign agreements, and a
question cannot be traced to an employer from the outside. So this book will
not pretend otherwise.

What follows are questions that come up again and again across the two
credible public sources, both free:
[*Introduction to Machine Learning Interviews*](https://huyenchip.com/ml-interviews-book/)
by Chip Huyen [@huyen2021interviews], which states that most of its
questions have been asked in real machine-learning interviews but attributes
none of them to a named company; and
[Machine Learning Interviews](https://github.com/alirezadir/Machine-Learning-Interviews),
compiled by an engineer from his own loops at several large technology
companies, which grounds the *topics* without tagging individual questions.
Where a question corresponds to a system a company has actually documented,
that system is cited so you can check the claim yourself.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the weighting

**Q: Explain TF-IDF to someone who has not seen it. Then explain why the
IDF term uses a logarithm.**

Give the two-factor decomposition first: a word matters here if it is
frequent in this document and rare across the collection. Then give the
information-theoretic answer from the intuition check above —
$\log(n/\mathrm{df})$ is the self-information of the term — and mention
diminishing returns. If you add that Spärck Jones proposed it empirically in
1972 [@sparckjones1972statistical] and the theory came later
[@robertson2004understanding], you have shown that you read primary
sources.

**Q: When would raw term counts outperform TF-IDF?**

When document frequency is not informative about importance. Examples: a
corpus of near-identical documents where every term has similar df; very
short texts where each term appears once anyway so TF adds nothing;
generative models like multinomial naive Bayes, whose likelihood is defined
over counts and whose probabilistic interpretation TF-IDF breaks. Also when
you need interpretable, additive counts for a downstream statistical test.

**Q: You add bigrams and accuracy drops. What happened?**

Variance. The feature space grew by roughly an order of magnitude while the
data stayed fixed, so most bigrams are seen once or twice and contribute
noise. The experiment in this chapter shows exactly this: 32,318 → 249,522
features, 0.831 → 0.819 accuracy. Fixes: raise `min_df`, strengthen
regularization, or restrict to bigrams that pass a pointwise-mutual-
information threshold.

**Q: Why does removing stop words sometimes hurt a sentiment model?**

Because stop word lists are built for topic retrieval, where function words
carry no signal, and sentiment is not topic. The standard lists delete
*not*, *no*, *never*, *very*, *only* and *but* — precisely the words that
invert or intensify an opinion. *This is not good* and *this is good* become
the same vector. The chapter's own numbers show both sides: stop word
removal gained 2.2 accuracy points on topic classification, and would lose
badly on the negation example. The rule to state out loud is that
preprocessing must be chosen against the task, never applied by default.

**Q: How does the curse of dimensionality show up in text, specifically?**

Sparsely. A TF-IDF matrix can have 10⁵ dimensions and 0.3% density, so
almost every pair of documents shares almost no non-zero coordinates and
distances concentrate — everything looks roughly equally far from everything
else. Note the twist that makes text unusual: the dimensionality is enormous
but so is the sparsity, which is why linear models with strong
regularization work far better on text than the raw dimension count would
suggest [@joachims1998text]. The escape routes are feature selection
(`min_df`), projection (truncated SVD), and learning a dense representation
instead (@sec-embeddings).

### Testing whether you understand the geometry

**Q: Why cosine similarity instead of Euclidean distance for documents?**

Length invariance — see the intuition check. The strong follow-up answer is
that on L2-normalized vectors the two are monotonically equivalent via
$\lVert a-b\rVert^2 = 2 - 2\cos(a,b)$, so the question is really about
whether you normalized.

**Q: Two documents have cosine similarity 0. What does that mean, and how
likely is it in practice?**

They share no terms at all. In a real corpus with stop words retained this
is nearly impossible, because every document contains *the*. If you are
seeing many zeros, you have probably over-aggressively filtered, or your
documents are extremely short — which is itself a signal to move to dense
representations (@sec-embeddings).

**Q: Your document-term matrix is 10⁶ × 10⁵. How do you store and work with
it?**

Compressed sparse row. Quote the density: text matrices run around 0.1–1%
non-zero, so the saving is two to three orders of magnitude. Then mention
the operations that *break* sparsity — mean-centering, PCA on the raw matrix
— and the ones designed to preserve it, notably truncated SVD, which is
latent semantic analysis and the historical bridge to @sec-embeddings.

### Testing whether you have shipped something

**Q: You trained a text classifier that performs well offline and badly in
production. Walk me through your debugging.**

The expected structure is a checklist, in cost order: (1) train/serve skew —
is the *identical* preprocessing pipeline running in both places, including
the vectorizer artifact and its IDF vector? (2) Vocabulary drift — new
product names, new error codes, all mapping to nothing. (3) Distribution
shift in the label mix. (4) A leak in the offline evaluation, such as
fitting the vectorizer before the train/test split. (5) Only then, the
model. Mentioning that the vectorizer is a *fitted artifact* that must be
versioned and shipped alongside the weights is the single answer that most
distinguishes practitioners from students.

**Q: Design a system to detect near-duplicate documents in a corpus of 100
million.**

They are testing whether you know not to compute 10¹⁶ pairwise similarities.
The expected answer is shingling plus MinHash plus locality-sensitive
hashing, giving approximate similarity in near-linear time. This chapter's
material is the front half of that pipeline: shingles are character or word
n-grams from exactly the tokenization decisions discussed above.

**Q: Build a search engine for internal technical documentation. Where do
you start?**

Start with BM25 [@robertson2009probabilistic] via Elasticsearch or a similar
engine, because it is a strong baseline that ships this week and handles
exact matches on part numbers that embeddings destroy. Measure it. Then add
dense retrieval for paraphrase and combine the two — hybrid retrieval, the
architecture you will build in @sec-rag. Candidates who jump straight to
embeddings without a lexical baseline are giving the wrong answer to a
question about engineering judgment.

**Q: Your Turkish (or Arabic, or Finnish) product costs far more per request
than the English one. Explain and fix.**

Tokenizer unfairness: the tokenizer was trained on mostly-English data, so
morphologically rich languages fragment into more tokens
[@petrov2023language]. The numbers in this chapter — 1.82× on `cl100k_base`,
1.39× on `o200k_base` — are the kind of concrete evidence that makes this
answer credible. Fixes, in increasing order of effort: pick a model whose
tokenizer has better coverage; measure cost in tokens per *task* rather than
per request; for a large enough deployment, train a domain and language
specific tokenizer.

### Testing depth on tokenization

**Q: Explain BPE. What happens to a word the tokenizer has never seen?**

Describe the merge loop, then answer the real question: nothing special
happens, which is the point. The word decomposes into known subwords, in the
worst case single characters, so there is no `<UNK>` token and no
information is discarded. Use the worked example from this chapter —
`lowest → low + est` from a model that never saw `lowest`.

**Q: Stemming versus lemmatization — and would you use either today?**

Define both, then give the modern answer: usually neither, because subword
tokenization addresses the same sparsity problem without a
language-specific rule set, and because transformers handle inflection
directly. Reserve them for genuinely sparse-model settings or for
morphologically rich languages where you have a good analyser
[@oflazer1994two]. Interviewers are checking whether you apply techniques by
habit or by argument.

## Where to go deeper

**Textbooks.**

- **[Speech and Language Processing](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)**,
  Jurafsky & Martin [@jurafsky2025slp]. The standard reference, free and
  continuously revised. For this chapter:
  [Chapter 2, *Words and Tokens*](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/2.pdf)
  (tokenization, normalization, Zipf, BPE) and
  [Chapter 5, *Embeddings*](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/5.pdf)
  (TF-IDF, cosine, PPMI). Note that the chapters were renumbered in the
  January 2026 draft — older blog posts pointing you at "Chapter 6 for vector
  semantics" are now out of date.
- **[Introduction to Information Retrieval](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/irbook.html)**,
  Manning, Raghavan & Schütze [@manning2008introduction]. The definitive
  treatment of the vector space model, and free in full. The single most
  useful page for this chapter is
  [the one on inverse document frequency](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/inverse-document-frequency-1.html)
  — it is the careful version of our "why the logarithm" argument. See also
  [stemming and lemmatization](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/stemming-and-lemmatization-1.html)
  and [BM25](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/okapi-bm25-a-non-binary-model-1.html).
- **[Text Mining with R: A Tidy Approach](https://www.tidytextmining.com/tfidf.html)**,
  Silge & Robinson [@silge2017text]. If you come from statistics and think
  in data frames rather than matrices, this chapter on TF-IDF may click
  faster than any of the above. Free online.

**Tokenization, hands on.**

- **[Hugging Face LLM Course, Chapter 6](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter6/1)**.
  Builds BPE, WordPiece and Unigram tokenizers and explains which models use
  which. [The BPE lesson](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter6/5)
  is the direct sequel to our toy implementation.
- **[minbpe](https://github.com/karpathy/minbpe)** and the accompanying
  [two-hour video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zduSFxRajkE), Andrej
  Karpathy [@karpathy2024minbpe]. A few hundred lines of clean Python that
  build a GPT-grade tokenizer from scratch. If you do one thing from this
  list, do this one.
- **[The Tokenizer Playground](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Xenova/the-tokenizer-playground)**.
  Paste text, switch tokenizers, watch the splits. Try your own name, your
  company's part numbers, and a paragraph of Turkish.
- **[tiktoken](https://github.com/openai/tiktoken)**. The library used for
  the cost measurements in this chapter.

**Reference documentation and courses.**

- **[scikit-learn: text feature extraction](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/feature_extraction.html#text-feature-extraction)**
  [@pedregosa2011scikit]. Documents the exact smoothed TF-IDF variant used
  here, which differs from the textbook formula — read it once properly and
  most "why don't my numbers match the book" questions disappear. The
  [20 Newsgroups classification example](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/text/plot_document_classification_20newsgroups.html)
  is a runnable, extended version of our experiment.
- **[Stanford CS276, Information Retrieval and Web Search](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs276/)**.
  Of all the public course pages, this is the closest match to this
  chapter's scope. [CS224N](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/) picks up
  where @sec-embeddings begins.
- **[NLP Course For You](https://lena-voita.github.io/nlp_course/word_embeddings.html)**,
  Elena Voita [@voita2020nlpcourse]. The clearest visual explanation of the
  move from sparse counts to dense vectors.
- **[Introduction to Machine Learning Interviews](https://huyenchip.com/ml-interviews-book/)**,
  Chip Huyen [@huyen2021interviews]. Free, and the most honest guide to what
  these interviews actually contain.

## Exercises

1. **Tokenizer economics.** Take a paragraph of your own technical writing
   in Turkish and its English translation. Using the Tokenizer Playground or
   `tiktoken`, count tokens under two different tokenizers. Compute the cost
   ratio, then estimate what that ratio does to your annual API bill at
   100,000 requests per month.
2. **Break the vectorizer.** Fit a `CountVectorizer` on ten documents from
   your own domain and print `get_feature_names_out()`. Find at least two
   tokens that are wrong — a destroyed identifier, a merged pair, a lost
   unit. Fix them with `token_pattern` and report what changed.
3. **Derive it by hand.** For the four-document corpus in this chapter,
   compute the TF-IDF vector for d3 with pen and paper, then verify against
   `TfidfVectorizer`. If they disagree, the disagreement is always in the
   smoothing — find it.
4. **Replicate and extend.** Reproduce the classification table above, then
   add one row: TF-IDF with `min_df=5`. Does accuracy fall? By how much did
   the feature count fall? Argue for one of the two configurations to a
   colleague who has to maintain it.
5. **Find the negation failure.** Construct two documents from your own
   field with opposite operational meaning and cosine similarity above 0.9
   under TF-IDF. Then write the sentence you would put in a design review
   explaining why this model must not be used for that decision.
6. **Zipf on your own data.** Plot rank against frequency on a log-log scale
   for a corpus you own. Does the line look straight? What are the top five
   tokens, and is any of them an artifact like `'ax`?
7. **The interview exercise.** Work through the five-document TF-IDF ranking
   problem in
   [§8.2.1 of Chip Huyen's book](https://huyenchip.com/ml-interviews-book/contents/8.2.1-natural-language-processing.html)
   with pen and paper, including its follow-up: if one document mentions the
   query term three times instead of once, what happens to its rank, and is
   that a desirable property of TF-IDF? Then check yourself with
   `TfidfVectorizer`. The follow-up is really a question about term-frequency
   saturation, which is exactly what BM25 adds and what `sublinear_tf`
   approximates.
